nodes.title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
nodes.authors: Shitong Liu, Xu Yang, Jingwei Zhang, Sheng Lian, Xinyu Zhuang, Kaiwen Guo, Quan Liu, Chunhai Zhao, Jiaxin He, Fan Yang, Manli Tao, Tingyu Yuan, Hongwei Shi, Chaomin Guo, Xiao-jing Liu, Zhuang Xiong, Feichan Yang, Xiangyu Zhu, Jinqiao Wang, Chaoyang Zhao, Zhiyong Liu
nodes.summary: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.

nodes.title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment
nodes.authors: Xueqing Liu, Young Hyun Cho, Bhanu Teja Gullapalli, Predrag Klasnja, Susan Murphy
nodes.summary: Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.

nodes.title: Unified Heterogeneous Feature Interaction via Effective-Rank Scaling for Recommender Systems
nodes.authors: Ao Zhang, Haochuan Li, Boya Du, Jian Yang, Qihang Fang, Yulin Xu
nodes.summary: Large-scale industrial ranking models must jointly capture heterogeneous feature interactions, long-term user behaviors, and multi-scenario dependencies under stringent online serving constraints. Existing architectures typically process sequential and non-sequential features with separate modules, limiting bidirectional information exchange. Directly applying homogeneous self-attention to all semantic tokens can also be inefficient when sequential and non-sequential signals exhibit different effective-ranks (eRanks). Meanwhile, shared representations can overlook scenario-specific patterns and induce negative transfer between scenarios. In this paper, we propose HiRank, a unified framework for multi-scenario recommendation that jointly models Heterogeneous feature Interactions via effective-Rank scaling. HiRank integrates gated sequential attention with heterogeneous feature interaction within a unified backbone, enabling bidirectional fusion between sequential and non-sequential representations. HiRank further uses scenario-aware aggregation to compress heterogeneous low-order tokens into a compact representation. Distinct learned projections transform the full compact representation into scenario-aware composite tokens with complementary global feature views and more uniform information density, enabling more effective high-order self-attention. Extensive experiments on industrial-scale datasets demonstrate favorable performance scaling with parameter count and consistent improvements over competitive baselines. Online A/B tests further show a 2.27% increase in orders per user.

nodes.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization for Agentic Robotics
nodes.authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch, Thomas Neff
nodes.summary: Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra now directly control robots and can generalize better than vision-language-action models (VLAs). We argue that this ability could arise from two distinct, composable skills: semantic reasoning, to understand what a task asks for in a scene, and motion control, to move the robot to do it. We show that small open VLMs are already capable of the first and mainly lack the second. We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches this missing motion skill, entirely in simulation on simple primitive tasks and from the model's own successes, with no frontier teacher or distillation and no real-world robot data. ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper, and 74.0% on a bimanual adaptation of RoboLab-120, on par with GPT-6 Astra's 72.2%. ZAP also generalizes to new objects, goals, and strategies, and in simulation to a robot embodiment on which it never trained.

nodes.title: SPARTA: A Sparse Ternary LLM Accelerator with Adaptive Attention and Unified Datapath for Long-Context Edge Inference
nodes.authors: Yanzhen Zhou, Zhengyu Han, Qunyou Liu, Zheyu Yan, Weihong Xu, Cheng Zhuo
nodes.summary: LLMs on edge devices are constrained by limited memory and bandwidth. Although 1.58-bit ternary weights greatly reduce model storage, long-context inference is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache traffic and attention. Existing accelerators also use separate datapaths for ternary linear layers and attention, incurring hardware and execution overhead. We present SPARTA, a sparse ternary LLM accelerator for efficient long-context edge inference. SPARTA integrates: (1) a phase-aware sparse dataflow exploiting heterogeneous sparsity across compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode; (2) a unified compute fabric mapping ternary SpMM/SpMV and bit-serial attention onto shared processing elements to exploit zero-weight and zero-bit sparsity; and (3) an adaptive two-stage attention engine combining page-level Top-k selection to reduce K-cache accesses with token-level Top-p pruning to reduce V-cache traffic. SPARTA reduces KV traffic by 4.1-4.8x over full attention and 1.3-1.5x over a state-of-the-art sparse-attention scheme, with task-dependent quality loss. Compared with NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, SPARTA achieves 3.9x higher generation throughput and 8.3x higher end-to-end energy efficiency on average; versus AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, the gains are 5.0x and 81.7x. It also delivers 1.6-12.0x higher throughput, 2.0-4.2x higher energy efficiency, and 1.3-51.4x higher area efficiency than FIGLUT, TeLLMe, and MCBP.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: AutoEnergyDesign: An LLM-Driven Agent for Automatic Energy System Design Optimization
nodes.authors: Amedeo Buonanno, Salvatore Fabozzi, Maria Valenti
nodes.summary: The design optimization of building energy systems represents a complex, high-dimensional search problem involving discrete technology selections, continuous sizing parameters, and intricate economic trade-offs in which every candidate must be evaluated by a year-long simulation. This paper presents AutoEnergyDesign, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) agent reasons over past simulation results, proposes configuration changes and learns in context from each outcome, while a git-based mechanism reverts changes that do not improve the design. The agent couples a reasoning model with explicit memories, a constrained action interface, and an environment-grounded keep/revert feedback signal. The simulator covers eight technologies and computes the 25-year Net Present Cost (NPC). On a case study with measured building loads, the agent, instantiated with three Claude models (Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5; ten runs of 50 simulations each), is compared with random search, Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Bayesian optimization and a (1+1) evolution strategy that shares the agent's acceptance rule (ten seeds of 300 evaluations). With all three models the agent reaches an NPC of 3.53MEUR, 1.20% and 0.23% below the best results of TPE and of the evolution strategy, and comes within 1% of it after a median of 18 to 27.5 simulations; among the baselines, only the evolution strategy does so, after a median of 192 evaluations. Every decision is recorded, making the search auditable.

nodes.title: Improving Signals, Declining Encoder: A Known-Answer Test of Label-Free Monitoring in Self-Supervised Learning
nodes.authors: Nilotpal Kakati
nodes.summary: Self-supervised training is monitored without labels, through the loss and statistics of the learned features. We report a case where we know the encoders lost part of what they had learned, so we can check whether these signals noticed. We trained LeJEPA encoders on synthetic images with known generating factors. In nine of ten seeds, the readability of those factors fell abruptly and stayed down, nearly always along the same direction in factor space. Meanwhile the loss kept falling, and most of the eleven label-free signals we tracked kept improving and rated the declining runs better than runs that did not decline. Standard change-point detection rarely flagged the decline near its onset, and selecting checkpoints by these signals mostly chose ones after it.

nodes.title: Global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ Convergence of Multilevel Gradient-Regularized Newton Methods
nodes.authors: Nick Tsipinakis, Matthias Voigt
nodes.summary: We develop and analyze multilevel gradient-regularized Newton methods for unconstrained convex optimization with Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. By computing Newton corrections in lower-dimensional subspaces, the proposed methods aim to reduce computational costs while preserving the global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ convergence rate in function values of the full-space method. To establish this rate for multilevel methods, we introduce a class of row-nested restriction operators that ensures monotonicity of the reduced-gradient norms across levels. Numerical experiments with row-nested operators demonstrate convergence behavior comparable to full-space gradient-regularized Newton, while offering substantial computational savings on large-scale instances.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: Program-Level Adversarial Co-Adaptive Self-Play for Robotic Security
nodes.authors: Leo Benaharon, Chi Zhang, Wei Zheng, Weifan Zhang, Yifan Wei, Yong Sun
nodes.summary: Coding agents can adapt robotic software by revising executable programs, but successful responses to an evolving opponent may not remain effective. We present a framework for program-level adversarial co-adaptive self-play in which coding agents generate attacks and defenses from tested opponent code and mission feedback, without model fine-tuning. Environment-specific interfaces support external programs for autonomous driving and SDK-level defenses for humanoid locomotion. Two eight-generation case studies reveal concrete software responses: a driving defender introduces direct-actuation recovery, while a humanoid defender revises incoming-state validation. These responses provide local task recovery but do not establish sustained robustness. The framework makes such adaptation and limitations observable through executable artifacts and task-level evidence.

nodes.title: Understanding and Repairing Cooperative Perception under Adverse Weather
nodes.authors: Mengxu Ma, Linshan Yan, Kailong Zhang, Ruiyang Guo, Dagang Shen, Yichen Fan, Hongping Gan
nodes.summary: A cooperative detector can lose a correct vehicle detection when surrounding LiDAR measurements change, even if the returns on the vehicle remain unchanged. We study this failure as Weather-Induced Context Interference. On our CoInfra development set, controlled removal outside annotated object boxes turns 22.1% of V2X-ViT's previously correct detections into misses. Restoring network features around the objects to their values before removal recovers 98.6% of these misses. The same restoration in each of three equally sized regions excluding the objects recovers none. Candidate analysis finds accurate boxes that are not selected, while other targets lack well-localized candidates. With paired reference features unavailable at inference, Adverse-Weather Cooperative Repair (AWCR) repairs candidates from current observations. A lightweight Local Correction head generates bounded alternatives, and Quality Selection ranks them alongside original boxes with a correction weight. In V2X-R simulation, AWCR also filters peer returns before detection using Point Classifier trained on generated-point labels. Candidate repair improves mean car BEV AP@0.7 by 4.22 points across three fits on natural adverse-weather CoInfra development inputs and vehicle AP@0.7 by 5.00 points on a rain-affected public recording. It also improves released HEAL, FadeLead, and V2X-DGW detectors with their pretrained weights fixed. On the full V2X-Radar-C validation benchmark, HEAL with AWCR achieves state-of-the-art LiDAR-only cooperative detection performance of 68.22 vehicle BEV AP@0.7.

nodes.title: GIFT: Representation Geometry Matters for Single-Domain Generalized Object Detection
nodes.authors: Yin Zhang, Yaoyue Zheng, Yongqiang Zhang, Bogdan Raducanu, Dan Liu
nodes.summary: Single-Domain Generalized Object Detection (S-DGOD) aims to generalize from a single source domain to unseen domains under distribution shifts. Existing efforts mainly focus on simulating unseen domains or suppressing domain-specific factors. However, they largely overlook the intrinsic generalization capability embedded in Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). In this work, we show that unconstrained fine-tuning disrupts the geometric structure of pre-trained representations, which encodes domain-invariant semantics. Motivated by this, we propose Geometric-Invariance Fine-Tuning (GIFT), a geometric-aware fine-tuning method for VFMs. Specifically, we introduce a series of learnable Householder reflections to the pre-trained weights to encourage geometry-consistent adaptation under domain shift. In addition, we propose a lightweight channel-wise scaling to facilitate effective task-specific adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GIFT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches on two S-DGOD benchmarks. Notably, by introducing fewer than 1% additional trainable parameters into the frozen backbone, the proposed method achieves improvements of +7.9% and +2.9% in mPC over the previous SOTA on the Cityscapes-C and Diverse Weather Dataset, respectively. This finding highlights that preserving representation geometry is crucial for robust cross-domain generalization, establishing GIFT as a principled and efficient solution to domain shift.

nodes.title: DynEdit: Dynamic Entropy-Guided Sequential Editing for Large Language Models
nodes.authors: Jinhu Fu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Li Sun, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Sen Su
nodes.summary: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.

nodes.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
nodes.authors: Xuan-Quy Dao, Le-Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Bich Le
nodes.summary: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering of the fixed baseline settings, mainly by moving BL-SMC from last to first. The ordering recurred on fresh realizations and did not change with 48 candidates, although BL-SMC's lead on the fresh set depends on a wider search range for its vertical switching gain. Reference preview reduced MPC tracking error and removed fallback activity on the figure-eight task. In single abrupt-step runs, completion depended jointly on fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in these profiles. We propose a reporting checklist that adds tuning effort, failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing to tracking accuracy.

nodes.title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
nodes.authors: Guoqiang Hu, Lichao Zhang, Yizhou Peng, Yuhao Luo, Haifeng Hu, Zhongqian Sun, Wei Yang, Eng Siong Chng
nodes.summary: When a user talks over a full-duplex dialogue model, it must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can improve this discrimination or change how readily it stops. In our GRPO runs the second dominates: no configuration lowers both error rates on more than one model, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better than their bases. We trace this partly to how the reward is estimated. The probability of stopping inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities the policy emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A group of rollouts that all agree gives no gradient, even when all fail; the push on the stop threshold is strongest where the model is unsure, whichever outcome is right; and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Confining the credit to the window removes only that leakage. Window likelihood (WL) samples the words but integrates over the stop decisions, so the probability of the correct outcome is computed exactly and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates by more than their confidence intervals, without talking into silence.

nodes.title: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review
nodes.authors: Sai Suresh Macharla Vasu, Sumedh Santosh Joshi, Philipp Christmann, Ivaxi Sheth, Ruta Binkyte, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Raouf Kerkouche, Hui-Po Wang, Mario Fritz
nodes.summary: The number of paper submissions to major AI conferences has increased dramatically in recent years, substantially increasing the peer-review workload of researchers. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support peer review, both by individual reviewers and by conference organizations. While LLM capabilities have improved considerably, their evaluations may be influenced by linguistic characteristics that are unrelated to scientific content. In this work, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying such effects by systematically perturbing the linguistic style of research papers. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic features associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high- or low-confidence linguistic features. To construct these interventions, we derive fine-grained rewriting instructions grounded in the linguistic literature and apply them using LLMs. Crucially, our interventions are designed to preserve the underlying scientific content. We then evaluate the resulting papers using different LLM reviewers. Our experiments expose a critical vulnerability in LLM-based peer review: reviewers systematically reward confident rhetoric independent of scientific content, raising serious concerns about the robustness of their assessments.

nodes.title: EmbodiedLab: Beyond Manipulation, Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know
nodes.authors: Hongcheng Gao, Zelin Zheng, Alex Zhou, Jay Zhu, Shijia Ge, Yazhe Wang, Xiping Li, Jianshu Zeng, Di Wu, Xuan Shangguan, Yexing Wan, Lingyu He, Yongli Wang, Xiaohan Yu, Zhiqi Jia, Yue Liu, Bryan Hooi, Yinpeng Dong, Wentao Zhang, Sihang Wu, Xiao He
nodes.summary: Physical action not only changes the state of an environment but is also the way to know its hidden properties: what cannot be seen must be inferred from the feedback to the change. As embodied agents advance from executing procedures to pursuing goals, success depends on properties neither given nor visible, so they must act to know. Existing benchmarks separate changing from knowing: manipulation benchmarks give the target state, so nothing has to be found out, whereas exploration and discovery benchmarks let the agent find out by looking or querying, so nothing physical has to be changed. Quantitative science experiments offer a natural testbed: the properties sought are new in every instance, appear only in instrument readings under conditions the agent sets up, and can be checked exactly. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a simulated laboratory of 35 such experiments. Given only a goal, the agent must decide what to measure, operate the apparatus with a robot arm, read instruments through cameras and judge when its readings suffice. Its 30 determination tasks specify what to find out, whereas its 5 optimization tasks ask only for the best result the apparatus allows. With native control, the strongest of seven frontier agents succeeds on 41.4% of the tasks. Ablations reveal two bottlenecks: contact-rich manipulation, where ground-truth depth and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, whereas executing every operation for the agent on five of the tasks raises it from at most 20% to at least 70%, so what an agent can know is bounded by how reliably it acts; and closed-loop experimental rigor, where with manipulation supplied, agents fail to gather sufficient readings or read instruments accurately, and most optimization runs stop at one design. Beyond evaluation, EmbodiedLab offers a resamplable environment with verifiable rewards for training embodied agents.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: OVM-Occ: Open-Vocabulary Monocular Occupancy Prediction via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Distillation
nodes.authors: Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, Guang Li
nodes.summary: Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.
nodes.subject: Gaussian Splatting

nodes.title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
nodes.authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki, Boris Jutzi, Kwanghee Won, Kyle Gao
nodes.summary: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense scene geometry from multiple images using feed-forward networks, but are typically designed for pinhole cameras. This assumption is embedded in the backbone itself: positional encoding locates each patch by its pixel index and the training loss weights every pixel equally, so both treat image coordinates as if they fixed the viewing direction in 3D space, which holds only for pinhole cameras. We condition both on the dense ray field, which maps each pixel to its 3D viewing direction and represents any central camera regardless of its projection model. $\textit{Angular coordinates}$ use the viewing direction of each patch for positional encoding, and $\textit{solid-angle weighting}$ scales the point loss by the angular area covered by each pixel. Together, they allow the same encoding and supervision to be used across different camera models. $\textbf{Any3R}$ is therefore a feed-forward model that reconstructs from any mix of central cameras without lens-specific retraining. On a benchmark of eight central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. $\textbf{Any3R}$ enables 3D reconstruction from crowdsourced and archival image collections containing diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/
nodes.subject: 3D Vision

nodes.title: PosePlaner: Denoising Any Feed-Forward Pose Predictor from Pairwise Planar Geometry
nodes.authors: Yihang Chen, Bin Tan, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu, Nan Xue
nodes.summary: Recent multi-view Transformers (e.g., DUSt3R and VGGT) have advanced 3D reconstruction by scaling training data and model capacity from two views to many views and long sequences, subsuming the classical SfM/SLAM pipeline of feature extraction, matching, and pose estimation in a single feed-forward pass. Yet this subsumption hides the interfaces between pipeline stages---correspondences, geometry, and pose are entangled in a single forward pass, leaving supervised fine-tuning as the major path to improvement and offering no mechanism to correct predictions from geometric evidence at test time. We propose PosePlaner to close this gap by reviving the classical coupling between correspondences and pose via flow matching, treating pose refinement as a conditional generation problem that takes coarse geometric matches and initial pose as input condition and fuses the resulting pose hypotheses into a single refined estimate, providing a continuous, data-driven analog of RANSAC voting. Our method is trained efficiently on two-view data, yet serves as a periodic refiner for streaming n-view pose estimators with no retraining. Empirically, it corrects failures of feed-forward predictors, substantially improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces accumulated drift in long streaming sequences.
nodes.subject: 3D Vision

nodes.title: The Voice on the Line
nodes.authors: Husein Zolkepli
nodes.summary: A transcriber listening through one microphone also hears everyone near it. We train causal voice isolators that keep only the caller for a speech recogniser: masking transformers with 20 ms of latency that enroll the caller from the call itself. Short evaluation windows hide two failures that real calls expose: forgetting the caller when another voice talks alone for a while, and damaging a caller who is alone. Long calls with turns, memory beyond the attention window and real headset crosstalk address the first, at a cost to the second. WavLM-Large's own weights, made causal and trained inside the model, move that trade, and training windows cut from longer calls remove most of a lone caller's cold start. The release (555M parameters) makes 16.13% word errors on 60 s AMI windows, against 23.66% for VoxLock, the strongest open isolator, and 14.77% on average over nine test sets, against 18.04%; it is level on Krisp's benchmark, and a caller who is alone still loses more words than with VoxLock. Distilled without WavLM into 22.1M and 9.8M parameters, it runs live on one CPU thread inside a LiveKit agent, at 12.5% and 8.5% of a core per call, with 10.66% and 10.99% error on our development sets (the release 10.49%). In an agent that talks back, noise interrupts it 0.54 times a minute of its speech behind our agent model, which gates its output on a caller-presence head, against 1.18 for VoxLock. We open-source the models, with a LiveKit plugin, at https://huggingface.co/collections/Scicom-intl/voice-isolator.

nodes.title: Style over Substance? Linguistic Bias in LLM-based Peer Review
nodes.authors: Sai Suresh Macharla Vasu, Sumedh Santosh Joshi, Philipp Christmann, Ivaxi Sheth, Ruta Binkyte, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Raouf Kerkouche, Hui-Po Wang, Mario Fritz
nodes.summary: The number of paper submissions to major AI conferences has increased dramatically in recent years, substantially increasing the peer-review workload of researchers. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support peer review, both by individual reviewers and by conference organizations. While LLM capabilities have improved considerably, their evaluations may be influenced by linguistic characteristics that are unrelated to scientific content. In this work, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying such effects by systematically perturbing the linguistic style of research papers. Specifically, we rewrite papers to exhibit (i) linguistic features associated with native or non-native English writing, and (ii) high- or low-confidence linguistic features. To construct these interventions, we derive fine-grained rewriting instructions grounded in the linguistic literature and apply them using LLMs. Crucially, our interventions are designed to preserve the underlying scientific content. We then evaluate the resulting papers using different LLM reviewers. Our experiments expose a critical vulnerability in LLM-based peer review: reviewers systematically reward confident rhetoric independent of scientific content, raising serious concerns about the robustness of their assessments.

nodes.title: Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
nodes.authors: Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He
nodes.summary: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose a control barrier function (CBF) framework using split covariance intersection (SCI) to fuse neighbor ranges and generate covariance-derived uncertainty scales for mapping and control. Pairwise constraints incorporate inter-step relative displacement to establish continuous-time safe-set invariance across discrete control steps under stated containment, feasibility, and synchronization conditions. A hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. Sequential local quadratic programs using preceding-UAV commands complete a 14-UAV search in 221.1 s with 0.45 m root-mean-square localization error while satisfying all separation and reference bounds. Comparisons across search regions, swarm sizes, sampled robust CBF, localizability and formation targets, and model predictive control quantify speed-accuracy-margin trade-offs. Tests on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, a typical UAV onboard computer, verify sub-4 ms mean control cycles and sub-5 ms mean full per-UAV onboard cycles, while Gazebo quadrotor flights verify mission completion and constraint compliance under over-water multipath, beacon-UAV drift, wind turbulence, yaw errors, and communication faults.

nodes.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
nodes.authors: Junyan Huang, Sanskar Agmain, Chen Gong, Yan Pang, FNU Suya
nodes.summary: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

nodes.title: OVM-Occ: Open-Vocabulary Monocular Occupancy Prediction via Geometry-Aware Vision-Language Distillation
nodes.authors: Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, Guang Li
nodes.summary: Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.

nodes.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
nodes.authors: Junho Kim, CheHyun Lee, Donghun Kang, Youngho Cho, Dongwook Lee, Heeseung Kim, Sungroh Yoon
nodes.summary: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.

nodes.title: The German Tank Problem & Navigating by Scent
nodes.authors: Kordel Kade France
nodes.summary: A robot searching for the source of an odor must eventually answer a notably hard question: have I arrived? Near the source, concentration gradients homogenize, turbulence corrupts the signal, and a small robot often lacks the positional accuracy to map the plume. Here, we describe a lightweight remedy inspired by a World War II statistics conundrum: the German tank problem. To approximate German armament production, Allied analysts developed an estimator based on serial numbers from captured tanks. Analogously, we use the same procedure over sampled chemical sensor readings from a robot to create estimates for the peak concentration of an odor plume, and therefore the odor's source. Treating each sensor reading as an observation, our unbiased estimator needs only a running maximum and a sample counter. A confidence bound turns both numbers into a principled rule that the robot or UAV can use to determine whether it should keep searching for the odor source. We derive the estimator and its bound, demonstrate its sample efficiency, and examine its robustness even when its assumptions fail. Finally, we summarize the estimator's role as the termination criterion for olfactory navigation.

nodes.title: CropReward: A Human-Preference Benchmark and Reward Model for Aesthetic Image Cropping
nodes.authors: Xiangfei Sheng, Xiaofeng Pan, Leida Li, Qian Zhang, Biao Wang, Johan Wagemans, Weisi Lin
nodes.summary: Aesthetic image cropping (AIC) aims to improve image composition and aesthetic quality by removing extraneous or distracting content. Over the past decade, AIC methods have evolved from specialized vision models to multimodal large language models(MLLMs). Reliable evaluation that reflects human preferences is essential for benchmarking AIC methods and guiding model optimization. However, the current AIC evaluation relies largely on geometry-based metrics such as intersection over union (IoU), as well as image aesthetic assessment(IAA) models. Although inconsistencies with human preferences have long been observed, the robustness and reliability of these evaluation criteria remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we first construct CropBench, a large-scale benchmark comprising 106,995 human preference pairs for 1,019 images, with each candidate set containing the original image and candidate crops produced by 14 AIC methods. A systematic study on CropBench reveals that the existing criteria, ranging from IoU to off-the-shelf IAA assessment models, only exhibit limited alignment with human preferences. Building upon CropBench, we further propose CropReward, an MLLM-based reward model that evaluates a candidate crop by comparing with the original uncropped image and outputs a score indicating explicit aesthetic improvement or degradation relative to the original. In addition, we employ CropReward to construct CropReward-300k, the largest AIC dataset to date, and further develop CropAlign, a preference-aligned AIC model trained solely with CropReward supervision, without human-annotated crop boxes. Experimental results demonstrate that CropReward aligns with human preferences significantly better than AIC existing criteria. CropAlign also surpasses the state-of-the-art AIC methods, demonstrating the advantage of CropReward in guiding AIC model optimization.

nodes.title: A Sign Law for Entropy Drift under Sampler Mismatch in RLVR
nodes.authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Jacob Steeves, Chang Liu
nodes.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), whether entropy rises or falls can depend on choices that matter little under exact sampling, such as whether over-length responses are masked or counted as failures. We trace this to sampler mismatch: rollouts are drawn with top-k/top-p truncation or at a temperature the learner does not apply. We prove that a constant advantage shift then changes the entropy of a softmax policy, at first order and in expectation, with a sign fixed by the sampler. Positive shifts sharpen the policy under any sampler whose likelihood ratio to the policy increases with token probability, including top-k, top-p, min-p, and temperatures below one, and flatten it under flatter samplers. In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-dependent part of this drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing can push to opposite signs. The rest comes from a covariance between advantages and the sampler's sharpness gap and feeds back on itself: in a two-level model, a push away from a sharper sampler takes off in finite time, while a pull toward it saturates. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling and indistinguishable from flat under exact sampling. Token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift, and four clipped minibatch updates per batch amplify it sevenfold. In 100-step runs, a net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion, and entropy raised at the start keeps rising only under truncation; cancelling the first-order drift at every step keeps entropy bounded without changing the learner. On a 9B reasoning model forked from an uncorrected run, zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner raises held-out accuracy after ten steps by 8.2 and 8.8 points over the uncorrected rule, with no difference under exact sampling.

nodes.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
nodes.authors: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
nodes.summary: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size N. On streaming replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types, and LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it regularly varying in N. A finite-pool form of this bound predicts the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold on held-out questions to within 6.1 points. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability. With a background drawn from the user's unfiltered history it keeps false alarms at 3-6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold; on LoCoMo it overshoots or turns conservative depending on where its reference cues come from. In a chronological replay with the user's own earlier messages as references, it speaks on 6-8% of session-opening turns, against 57% for the deployed gate at N=2048, at about 50 ms per decision on one CPU thread. A cross-encoder reranker pays the same price of scale, and on a prospective-memory benchmark, similarity gates recall at most 9% of constraints at controlled false alarms. One human and two LLM annotators judge most false alarms unhelpful for a response. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

nodes.title: MMFact: Simplifying Multimodal Misinformation Detection with Shared Resources and Tools
nodes.authors: Yuchen Miao, Zijun Wang, Mingtai Zhang, Xiaoyi Chen, Sihan Deng, Xianglin Ding
nodes.summary: Multimodal misinformation detection methods often rely on different preprocessing pipelines and auxiliary resources, making experimental comparisons difficult to interpret. We present MMFact, a collection of shared resources and tools that simplifies this research workflow. It brings together 47 detector implementations and baselines, three multimodal datasets, and prepared materials ranging from semantic features to OCR, image descriptions, and external evidence. Compatible methods can use the same materials, reducing variation introduced by preprocessing and supporting fairer comparisons. A modular training and evaluation framework preserves method-specific designs while providing common experimental procedures. By treating prepared materials as a shared research resource, MMFact helps researchers focus on developing and evaluating detection methods.

nodes.title: BEHAVIOR-Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
nodes.authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
nodes.summary: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.

nodes.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
nodes.authors: Fatma Ahmed Mansour, Rahatara Ferdousi, Manar Fathy Elshenawy
nodes.summary: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

nodes.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
nodes.authors: Skander Moalla, Ahmad Rammal, Niket Patel, Remi Munos, Julia Kempe
nodes.summary: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

nodes.title: LLM4Robot-Bench: How Far Can GPT-6 Astra Go in Robotic Manipulation? A Hierarchical, Matched Sim-Real Benchmark
nodes.authors: Haibao Yu, Jiaqi Meng, Zijian Zhang, Bowen Jing, Lei Yang, Yue Hu, Chenchen Ge, Yiming Hou, Chenbo Xin, Dawen Ye, Haifang Qin, Jin Li, Weitao Zhou, Jianing Qiu, Jiankai Sun, Dandan Zhang, Zaiqing Nie, Ping Luo, Ding Zhao
nodes.summary: We introduce LLM4Robot-Bench, a hierarchical, matched Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.

nodes.title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
nodes.authors: Haoyu Zhao, Xingyue Zhao, Zhian Su, Bohan Hou, Yinzhou Tang, Fengyi Wang, Kehan Li, Yuming Jiang, Zhenyu Zeng, Mingxiu Chen, Deli Zhao, Siteng Huang, Xin Li, Zhongyu Li
nodes.summary: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.

nodes.title: PS-DLO: Property- and Spatially Aware Deformable Linear Object Manipulation Policy
nodes.authors: Mengdi Li, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Yunfan Lou, Yifan Yang, Yuanpeng He, Xuan Han, Tao Liu, Zhibo Pang
nodes.summary: Deformable linear objects (DLO) pose a coupled perception and control challenge: their slender geometry makes precise localization difficult, while their deformations depend on object-specific physical properties. To address this challenge, we propose PS-DLO, a property- and spatially aware DLO manipulation policy. First, contrastive image-text learning maps the initial observation to categorical descriptions of DLO properties, providing explicit physical and structural priors for action generation. Second, SAM3 extracts mask-guided features from future observations, which are distilled into the policy's action expert to encode task-relevant DLO regions and their subsequent configurations. We evaluate PS-DLO on nine real-world tasks across single-arm and bimanual platforms, training a shared multi-task policy for each embodiment. PS-DLO achieves an average success rate of 68.9%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.0 percentage points. In generalization experiments, PS-DLO achieves higher success rates than the baseline in six of seven visual-shift conditions on butterfly-knot untying. These results demonstrate that combining object-property priors with future spatial supervision improves multi-task DLO manipulation and robustness to visual variation.

nodes.title: Multimodal Socially Aware Framework for Human-Robot Interaction in Virtual Reality
nodes.authors: Richard Xu, Dakarai Crowder, Alexis E. Block, Wenzhen Yuan
nodes.summary: Social robots must coordinate speech and movement while interpreting multimodal human input. We present a multimodal framework that integrates speech, vision, and touch to generate contextually appropriate robot speech and movement. We evaluated the framework in virtual reality with 18 participants across five social interaction scenarios, comparing its performance against a human-teleoperated baseline. Although participants rated the autonomous system above the neutral midpoint for both naturalness and social appropriateness, the teleoperated baseline received significantly higher ratings on both measures. Behavioral coding and qualitative feedback revealed that conversational timing, clarification of ambiguous requests, and spatial coordination were important factors contributing to this performance gap. These findings highlight key challenges in developing autonomous robots capable of natural, multimodal social interaction.

nodes.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
nodes.authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Sifna Nasar, Mariam Ahmed, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
nodes.summary: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release SurgBox, a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub
nodes.subject: Digital Human

nodes.title: How Much Do Structural Tools Help Small Coding Agents? A Pre-Registered Scale Study of Code Localization
nodes.authors: Saurav Bellam
nodes.summary: Code-graph and embedding tools are routinely added to LLM coding agents on the premise that they supply repository structure the model lacks. We report a pre-registered study of how much such tools help off-the-shelf agents localize the code an issue requires changing and how the benefit varies with model size. Nine open-weight models (Qwen3 0.6B to 32B, Gemma 4 E2B to 12B) run one fixed localization harness on 500 held-out SWE-bench tasks under four tool sets (grep only; plus embedding search; plus code-graph tools; both) and a placebo arm whose structural tools return random entities, with five sampled seeds per condition: 170,500 episodes under hypotheses, tests and claim criteria frozen before the runs. The tools raise canonical function Acc@10 by +0.06 to +0.10 for the Qwen3 models up to 14B and the two small Gemma 4 models, by +0.03 at 32B (a near miss after correction), and not at all for Gemma 4 12B, which rarely submits; the gain is larger for small models than for the largest model in both families. The placebo shows that the gain is caused by what the tools return rather than by having them, and that random tool output harms two small models. The pre-registered claim that a 4B model with tools matches a 32B model without them fails. Secondary analyses show that the embedding index, not the code graph, carries the gain; that the gain replicates on tasks created after every model's release and survives a shell harness, thinking mode, FP8 serving and a file-level metric that output formatting cannot inflate; and that it is mostly exposure: the tools show the gold code more often. Injecting the gold code directly explains the size trend. A 32B model already finds the code without the tools, so they add little exposure, while small models act on a shown answer less often (conversion 0.09, 0.24 and 0.40 at 1.7B, 4B and 32B). We release registration, code, episodes and analyses.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Semantic-Coupled Perception Framework for Autonomous Laparoscope Control
nodes.authors: Enduo Zhao, Fangzhou Li, Yujie Zhu, Sicheng Lu, Fang Chen, Longfei Ma, Hongen Liao
nodes.summary: In minimally invasive surgery (MIS), maintaining an appropriate field of view (FoV) is essential for surgical safety and efficiency. However, conventional autonomous laparoscope control methods often treat visual tracking and surgical phase recognition independently, limiting robustness under occlusion, entity overlap, and camera motion. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous laparoscope control framework that couples real-time surgical phase recognition with camera-motion-compensated visual perception. By exploiting phase-dependent relationships among surgical entities, the framework improves target state estimation under challenging visual conditions, supporting task-aware autonomous FoV control. Benchmark and phantom experiments evaluate the framework in surgical phase recognition, target tracking under occlusion and entity overlap, and autonomous FoV control, showing improved target visibility and task execution compared with fixed-FoV control. These results highlight the potential of incorporating task-level semantics into visual state estimation for autonomous laparoscope guidance.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Future Prediction as Training-Only Video Supervision for Pretrained VLA Policies
nodes.authors: Hanwen Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Qing Guo, Zhida Zhang, Chao Chen, Xi Chen, Jie Cao
nodes.summary:
World action models (WAMs) introduce predictive supervision into robot policy learning by jointly modeling future visual observations and actions. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire rich visual and semantic representations as well as action-generation capabilities. Their action objectives typically lack direct supervision for predicting future visual observations. Future videos in robot demonstrations record object motion and task progress. They can provide temporal visual supervision that complements action labels.
  We propose Training-Only Video Supervision, which introduces future-video prediction as an auxiliary objective for VLA fine-tuning. We condition a randomly initialized video-prediction expert on the VLA's shared vision-language features. The expert learns to predict future video latents from robot demonstrations. The video prediction loss and the original action loss jointly update the shared vision-language backbone, providing additional temporal visual supervision. After training, we remove the video expert and its adapter. The fine-tuned VLA retains its original action-generation pathway at inference. On the 50-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, our method achieves 71.18% average success, compared with $π_{0.5}$ of 58.33%. In a matched evaluation on four real-world manipulation tasks, success increases from 42.50% to 61.25%. These results show that future visual modeling can serve as auxiliary training supervision for pretrained VLAs. The fine-tuned action policy benefits from this supervision without retaining a video-prediction branch at deployment.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Entity Matching using Decision Models
nodes.authors: Aaron Steiner, Ralph Peeters, Christian Bizer
nodes.summary: Entity matching is the task of deciding whether two records describe the same real-world entity. Current methods often rely on pre-trained language models (PLMs), which require task-specific fine-tuning, or on generative large language models (LLMs), which need no fine-tuning but are more expensive and slower than PLMs at matching large numbers of records. Decision models are a new class of pre-trained models that return probabilities for predefined answer options rather than generate free-form text. This paper presents an extensive experimental evaluation of decision models for entity matching. We evaluate six decision models in a zero-shot setting on eight benchmarks and compare them to frontier generative LLMs and the fine-tuned PLM-based matcher Ditto. Without task-specific training data, the best decision model exceeds Ditto in mean F1 score and stays a few F1 points below the frontier LLMs at less than 1% of their cost. We show that three of the decision models produce well-calibrated match probabilities. We then explore two approaches to improving F1 scores at the expense of higher costs: First, we investigate model cascades that defer the least certain record pairs to a frontier LLM, increasing the mean F1-scores of the four strongest decision models by 2.7-4.8 percentage points. These cascades achieve F1-scores that do not differ significantly from those obtained by applying the frontier LLM to all record pairs, while reducing costs by factors of 2.5 to 5.1. Second, we employ an LLM to label a development set, which we use to select in-context demonstrations or to derive matching rules. These approaches raise the mean F1 score less than the model cascades. The cascade combining the best decision model with an ensemble of three frontier LLMs achieves an F1 score that does not differ significantly from that of the frontier LLM ensemble alone, at less than one-fifth of its cost.
