nodes.title: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
nodes.authors: Julius Erbach, Dominik Narnhofer, Bernt Schiele, Jan Eric Lenssen, Konrad Schindler
nodes.summary: We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78, improves MaskGen-KL-XL HPSv2 from 24.50 to 26.50, and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 4.5% to 56.6%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (41.0%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID, 27.80 HPSv2 and 96.7% accuracy.
nodes.subject: Digital Human

nodes.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
nodes.authors: John Kitaoka, Thao Amelia Pham, Carlos Rafael Giudice, Jacob Merizian
nodes.summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly under both their feedback monitor and GPT-5.6 Sol in at most 32% of executions, compared with 82% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
nodes.subject: Spatial Agents

nodes.title: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs
nodes.authors: Ori Press, Alexander Golubev
nodes.summary: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
nodes.authors: Nikita Tsoy
nodes.summary: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize industry profit and market welfare. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
nodes.authors: Elena Wittemyer, Grace Gao
nodes.summary: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
nodes.authors: Chloe Su, Jiahan Li, Zhenting Qi, Chaoran Cheng, Haoyu Chen, Sejoon Jun, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
nodes.summary: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
nodes.authors: Sergio Burdisso, Esaú Villatoro-Tello, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés, Yanis Labrak, Jordi Luque, Milos Cernak, Petr Motlicek
nodes.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
nodes.subject: LLM Agents with Reinforcement Learning

nodes.title: CoDeFont: One-Shot Font Generation via Multi-Scale Factor-Specific Representation Learning
nodes.authors: Rejoy Chakraborty, Prasun Roy, Saumik Bhattacharya, Umapada Pal
nodes.summary: One-shot Font Generation (OFG) aims to synthesize a target glyph by transferring the stylistic characteristics of a single reference glyph while preserving the structure of the target character. However, accurately capturing font style from a single reference image remains challenging due to the limited stylistic information available in a single glyph, and this challenge is further amplified for complex scripts. We propose CoDeFont, a script-agnostic OFG framework that addresses this challenge through multi-level style-content factorization and progressive style-content reconciliation. CoDeFont independently aggregates complementary style and structural information across multiple spatial levels to obtain factor-specific representations, while a contrastive objective explicitly encourages separation between style and content embeddings. During reconstruction, the disentangled representations are progressively injected through multi-level style conditioning, enabling stylistic information to be incorporated at different decoding resolutions while preserving the underlying glyph structure. We evaluate CoDeFont on structurally distinct Bengali and Latin scripts across seen and unseen font styles. Extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed framework for OFG across diverse writing systems.
nodes.subject: 3D Vision

nodes.title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
nodes.authors: Xin Zhang, Robby T. Tan
nodes.summary: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose FuseAdapt, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs adaptation-space fusion by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM), a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +11.25 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
nodes.authors: Ruibin Ju, Ruifeng Cai, Min Xu, Zhuojie Chen, Lin Wang
nodes.summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
nodes.authors: Sara Inácio, Hugo Proença, João C. Neves
nodes.summary: Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation improves pediatric performance on average, although the effect varies across models. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not necessarily indicate greater robustness to domain shift.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
nodes.authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Yiyang Lu, Katelyn Gan, Todd Zickler
nodes.summary: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.
nodes.subject: Spatial Agents

nodes.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
nodes.authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Han Wang, Shuo Zhang
nodes.summary: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill makes mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, but what it damages has not been measured. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions in four MoE families on short-answer question answering. At half the experts the F1 loss is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but no longer answers briefly. The loss is made at a few tokens: the two chat-template tokens before the answer in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and the first 8-32 tokens, where the instruction sits, in DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Keeping them at full experts removes most of the F1 loss and about half and a fifth of the increase in answer NLL. Reduction changes the first-token sink statistics by less than 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most a quarter of the loss. We then test placement on real prompts with about 4% of tokens at full experts. Putting them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while the same budget scattered in the documents is about 3 points worse in both prespecified primary tests of this comparison. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
nodes.authors: Bing Cheng, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Yifan Jin, Xinyi Chen, Ruifeng Tu, Shuhuai Wang, Tao Lin, Zhimu Zhou, Yuxin Du, Fangwei Zhong, Junchi Yan, Bo Zhao
nodes.summary: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations and leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families, three everyday scenes per task, and 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected via VR teleoperation with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. Experiments show that, among six representative policies, even the best-performing method achieves an average success rate of only 24.4%, highlighting the challenges existing methods face in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that, across the two tasks, joint Core + Gen training improves performance by 12% and 38%, respectively, over training on Core followed by fine-tuning on Gen, indicating that joint training makes better use of Core knowledge. With matched Core data, 8 Gen demonstrations achieve performance comparable to training on 16--32 Gen demonstrations alone. On all three tested Gen targets, functionally matched Core data yields greater gains in success rate than mismatched data. We release the Evo-DexBench dataset and benchmark to support the evaluation of dexterous manipulation policies' generalization across related tasks.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
nodes.authors: Dawei Li, Bohan Jiang, Huan Liu
nodes.summary: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.
nodes.subject: Embodied Intelligence

nodes.title: Hierarchical Building-Floo-Room Framework for Privacy-Preserving Autonomous Delivery in Large-Scale Buildings
nodes.authors: Xu Xiaoji, Chen Jinhua, Zhang Leihan, Luo Rui, Liao Zhongyuan
nodes.summary: Autonomous delivery in large scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building-Floor-Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter building and inter floor connectivity, room level access constraints, and privacy sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non interactive, privacy preserving delivery, supported by reachability aware distances and a closed loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: To Think or Not to Think: Pre-Decisional Reasoning Budgets for Referring Audio-Visual Segmentation
nodes.authors: Haojie Hu, Senda Chen, Ying Shen, Lin Zhang
nodes.summary: Multimodal reasoning systems increasingly assume that longer chain-of-thought (CoT) uniformly improves downstream grounding. We show that this assumption fails in referring audio-visual segmentation (Ref-AVS): simple queries can be harmed by excessive reasoning, creating an "overthinking trap" associated with phrase and localization drift, while genuinely ambiguous queries still benefit from multi-step reasoning. To systematically study this, we construct counterfactual reasoning-budget labels under a five-fold out-of-fold evaluation protocol. Our results recast adaptive Ref-AVS reasoning as a pre-decisional representation problem: before the first generated token, the generation-onset state contains linearly decodable information predictive of whether additional reasoning will improve segmentation. A linear probe predicts binary reasoning need with 70.1% accuracy, substantially outperforming text-only features and uncertainty-based proxy signals. As a router, the onset-state controller improves over downstream confidence routing and closely matches Short-then-Decide while using far fewer tokens. Proxy comparisons show that the onset representation contains predictive information not fully recovered by the evaluated hand-crafted features. Reusing this onset state for lightweight, single forward-pass routing reduces autoregressive token consumption by 60% while retaining about 96% of always-long performance. It further provides a cost-quality trade-off on $R^2$-AVSBench without target-label tuning, rather than an accuracy improvement over always-long. Error analysis links harmful long reasoning to phrase and localization drift, illustrating the benefit of bypassing unnecessary reasoning on simple queries. Ultimately, our results support efficient adaptive reasoning in Ref-AVS through pre-decisional internal representations.
nodes.subject: Multimedia

nodes.title: Modular Inverse Dynamics and Wrench Recovery for Closed-Chain Mechanisms Using Path Assembly
nodes.authors: Mohammad Dastranj, Jouni Mattila
nodes.summary: Rigid closed chains can admit indeterminate internal reactions even when their motion is fully specified. This paper develops a modular inverse-dynamics workflow that combines path-based motion reconstruction with recovery of uniquely determined actuator and joint-wrench outputs. Analytical second-order differentiation of assembled transformation paths supplies passive velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch. Spatial Newton--Euler balances are then assembled over the physical body-and-joint graph. Established nullspace and dual criteria identify and recover unique outputs, while balance, ideal-joint admissibility and affine-family diagnostics assess nonunique reference reactions. Evaluation against Simscape Multibody uses prescribed motion of a seven-degree-of-freedom heavy-duty hybrid serial--parallel manipulator under common rigid-body, ideal-joint assumptions. The results show close agreement with the reference for passive positions, actuator efforts and uniquely recoverable constraint-wrench components. Reaction diagnostics support compatibility with the admissible numerical load family.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: CtRoFlow: Monocular Camera-to-Robot Pose Estimation via Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
nodes.authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Zhiwei Fang, Rulin Zhou, Quanlu Zhang, Beilei Cui, Hongliang Ren
nodes.summary: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering, PnP based on predicted 2D keypoints with limited robustness or 3D registration which suffers from monocular scale ambiguity and complex training configuration. In this work, we propose CtRoFlow, a flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor (KFE) to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator (GCG), which generates condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-based Loss for decoupled training and scale consistency, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with multiple cameras, as well as for zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Code will be available upon acceptance.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
nodes.authors: Woocheol Shin, Taeyoung Yun, Jiwon Sung, Hyeongyu Kang, Jeongmin Park, Jaewoo Lee, Kyuil Sim, Dohyun Kim, Yutong He, Jinkyoo Park
nodes.summary: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
nodes.authors: Bing Cheng, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Yifan Jin, Xinyi Chen, Ruifeng Tu, Shuhuai Wang, Tao Lin, Zhimu Zhou, Yuxin Du, Fangwei Zhong, Junchi Yan, Bo Zhao
nodes.summary: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations and leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families, three everyday layouts per task, and 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected via VR teleoperation with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. We first compare few-shot adaptation strategies and find that joint Core + Gen training makes the most effective use of Core knowledge. Under this setting, we evaluate six representative policies. The best-performing policy, $π_{0.5}$, achieves a mean success rate of only 24.4%, revealing the limitations of existing methods in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that on the tested Gen targets, functionally matched Core data yields larger success-rate gains than mismatched data, and that with matched Core data, 8 Gen demonstrations reach the performance of training on 16--32 Gen demonstrations alone. These results indicate that Evo-DexBench separates knowledge transfer from task memorization under controlled conditions and effectively evaluates the generalization of dexterous manipulation policies across related tasks.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: SnapJudge: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text
nodes.authors: Yixuan Huang, Danish Pruthi, Bhuwan Dhingra
nodes.summary: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.
nodes.subject: Generative Search Engines

nodes.title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
nodes.authors: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee
nodes.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
nodes.authors: Ziye Mei, Haotian Ma
nodes.summary:
Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation?
  We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits.
  We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964.
  These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
nodes.authors: Haotian Ma, Ziye Mei, Frederic Sala
nodes.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
nodes.authors: Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang
nodes.summary: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
nodes.authors: Minhyeok Roh, Minseo Lee, Jun Young Jeong, Byeonghyeon Lee, Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Jaesik Park, Eunbyung Park
nodes.summary: Dynamic Gaussian representations enable high-quality, real-time volumetric video, with FreeTimeGS standing out as a high-performing approach. Nevertheless, challenging motion remains a persistent issue in dynamic Gaussian reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that these failures stem not from limited representational capacity alone, but also from where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. To address these limitations, we augment FreeTimeGS with two Gaussian allocation strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, then reinitializes low-opacity Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations inferred from multi-view observations, independently of their previous locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying FreeTimeGS representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly for small, rapidly moving objects and fine appearance details in highly dynamic regions.
nodes.subject: Gaussian Splatting

nodes.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
nodes.authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
nodes.summary: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but pursues a proxy that coincided with the intended goal during training instead of the goal itself. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents and what enables them to be recovered without retraining. We study this across eight visual navigation and manipulation tasks, including robot control. While tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, we uncover that the goal is lost at one of three different depths. This depth predicts which recovery works in each task. When the goal is followed, but outcompeted by the proxy, steering the existing policy redirects it to the goal's location, raising goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. When it is read, but not followed, steering fails, but a lightweight new downstream wiring recovers goal reach from 31.6% to 84.3%. When it is not read, none of the methods work, as the policy does not use the goal information. The same tracing also reveals what replaces the goal: functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, or cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. Knowing where the goal is lost tells us whether an agent can be repaired or has to be retrained. Goal misgeneralization should therefore be studied and evaluated inside the agent, not only from its behavior.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
nodes.authors: Fucai Zhu, Xidong Zhang, Yichi Zhang, Yipan Wang, Fubo Wang, Zibin Wu, Kaiqi Li, Jianhao Jiao, Shihan Lu, Di Hu, Mengdi Xu, Siyu Zhu, Xiaoxiao Long, Yao Yao, Xun Cao, Zhuo Xu, Koichi Hashimoto, Qifeng Chen, Zhe Li, Jianfei Yang, Haofei Lu, Danica Kragic, Shuicheng Yan, Jianghua Duan, Michael Yu Wang, Weihao Yuan
nodes.summary: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
nodes.authors: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi, Usha Bhalla, Thomas Icard, Matt Feiszli, Thomas McGrath, Vasudev Shyam, Demba Ba, Leon Bergen, Nina Miolane, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel
nodes.summary: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
nodes.authors: Chaemin Lee, Hae Min Cho
nodes.summary: Language-guided robot navigation under partial observability requires robots to reason over spatial-semantic evidence accumulated across observations, particularly when goals involve spatial relations between objects. This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework that integrates online mapping, persistent object--relation memory, and goal-conditioned navigation. Using RGB-D observations and SLAM, $S^3$-Nav maintains a persistent object--relation memory containing object records and confirmed relation records alongside an evolving navigation context containing exploration frontiers, without requiring a pre-existing map. A goal-conditioned evidence interface selects task-relevant evidence from this structured state and constructs a capacity-controlled decision view as part of the high-level policy input for exploration, target approach, and stopping decisions. The persistent memory remains available for subsequent reasoning and verification even when some of its records are excluded from the decision view. To ensure grounded execution, provisional policy decisions are independently validated against persistent object--relation memory and current geometric evidence before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks show improved closed-loop navigation reliability and reduced language-model token consumption with capacity-controlled evidence exposure under the evaluated inference configuration.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
nodes.authors: Qianru Meng, Xi Zhang, Konstantinos Papakostas, Congfeng Cao, Wenxiang Hu, Tianyi Lu, Xiao Zhang, Lun Zhou, Zaiqiao Meng, Zhaochun Ren, Xiaohui Yan, Yougang Lyu
nodes.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.

nodes.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
nodes.authors: Yuxuan Xia, Xiao-Tong Yuan
nodes.summary: Must the dimension and accuracy costs of zeroth-order optimization multiply? Global upper bounds for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization scale as $O(dε^{-4})$, with both factors separately necessary. We show that their product is unavoidable. We establish an $Ω(dε^{-4})$ lower bound for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, yielding an $Ω(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ bound for nonsmooth Goldstein stationarity. Both match the best-known full-space upper bounds, establishing joint minimax optimality in dimension and accuracy. These bounds hold against fully adaptive randomized algorithms with unrestricted queries and outputs, even under arbitrary sample reuse. As a byproduct, we establish noiseless exact-value lower bounds for both smooth and Goldstein stationarity, even against randomized algorithms.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: Feed-Forward Multi-View Feature Coding for 3D Gaussian Splatting
nodes.authors: Seungmi Choi, Ji-Hyoun Choi, Suhyun Jo, Tae-Gwon Park, Hui Yong Kim
nodes.summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods enable efficient reconstruction of 3D scenes from sparse multi-view images in a single forward pass, without scene-specific optimization. However, existing feed-forward scene-coding pipelines follow a "generate-then-compress" framework, first generating a Gaussian representation and then encoding its geometry and appearance through separate coding paths, complicating codec design and limiting the exploitation of cross-attribute redundancy. We propose multi-view feature coding for Gaussian splatting (MFGS), an end-to-end feed-forward framework for scene coding. Instead of compressing an explicit Gaussian representation, MFGS extracts multi-view features from the input images and encodes them into a compact bitstream. Through end-to-end rate-distortion training, MFGS learns a compact latent representation of multi-view features that jointly represents geometry and appearance, enabling the receiver to predict Gaussian attributes from the decoded features. We further introduce importance-guided Gaussian selection to accommodate different rendering budgets, allowing the receiver to adjust the number of Gaussians used for rendering from the same bitstream. Across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, MFGS achieves 99.76-99.86% bitrate savings over the generate-then-compress pipeline, as measured by BD-rate, while reducing total GMACs by 52-55% and providing an approximately 12 times end-to-end speedup.

nodes.title: PiCo: Physics-Informed Concept Probing for Geo-Foundation Models
nodes.authors: Yihang She, Andrew Blake, Jianbo Qi, Srinivasan Keshav
nodes.summary: Geo-foundation models (GFMs) are evaluated by downstream predictive performance. This reveals little about which physical properties their embeddings are sensitive to or which are used in predictions. This limits developers' ability to test hypotheses about model behaviour and users' ability to select models for new tasks. We propose Physics-Informed Concept Probing (PiCo), a post-hoc framework for explaining GFM predictions. PiCo identifies concept vectors in GFM embedding space using synthetic multispectral satellite observations from a 3D radiative transfer model coupled with a game engine. These vectors characterise GFM sensitivities to physical properties, informing domain-based hypotheses about downstream performance. Projecting embeddings onto concept vectors produces low-dimensional representations for quantifying concept importance in predictions. We evaluate PiCo on three GFMs with different input modalities using seven physical concepts covering forest leaf optics and canopy structure. In ground-cover estimation, RGB-only inputs reduce dry-matter sensitivity and disproportionately degrade predictions for dry vegetation and bare ground, as anticipated by PiCo's sensitivity analysis. For hierarchical forest type and tree species classification, concept representations retain 70.0--93.8% of full-embedding accuracy. Different GFMs capture physical differences between classes, such as canopy structure between broadleaf forest and cleared ground and leaf-water-content between oak and beech. Yet they differ in the strength of these contrasts and the concepts they use for classification. PiCo provides an interpretable basis for hypothesis testing and model assessment, with potential applicability beyond Earth observation wherever physical models enable controlled simulation and pretrained embeddings are accessible for probing. Code is available at https://github.com/yihshe/PiCo.git.

nodes.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
nodes.authors: Jasleen Kaur, Chloé Cachet, Koray Karabina, Jean Belo Klamti, Philippe Lamontagne
nodes.summary: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.

nodes.title: A wind memory for odour source search in reversing wind
nodes.authors: Junlong Shen, Shunsuke Shigaki
nodes.summary: After wind reversals, old odour arrives while the sensed wind points away from the source, so wind followers, which surge upwind, are misled. A hold gate stores the wind at first odour contact and feeds it to an unchanged follower while the live wind points over 90° away. On 60 random simulated reversing flows it raised a published moth model's success by 10.8 points (95% CI 6.6 to 15.4) and four other followers' by 6.0 to 10.1, but cost the moth model 5 points in steady wind. A fixed wind delay was not resolvably worse at insect scale, but in simulation rescaled to a legged robot's sensors and turn rate the gate beat the best delay for two followers, only one margin surviving Bonferroni correction. As the robot never ran the gate and a plain spiral searcher beat the gated moth model, it is an add-on, not a better searcher.

nodes.title: PingpongDuo: Agile Humanoid Table Tennis Doubles with Safe Team Coordination
nodes.authors: Haoran Jiang, Yichao Zhong, Kai Zhang, Cheng Liu, Yixuan Pan, Zhenjie Yang, Jingbo Wang, Tianyu Li, Li Chen
nodes.summary: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.

nodes.title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
nodes.authors: Matteo He, William F. Shen, Alex Iacob, Andrej Jovanovic, Xinchi Qiu, Nicholas D. Lane
nodes.summary: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

nodes.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
nodes.authors: Gwénolé Lecorvé, Delphine Charlet, Pierre Adam, Floriane Behanzin, Lionel Delphin-Poulat, Johannes Heinecke, Géraldine Damnati, Pelin Kaytmaz, Noureddine Khaous, Charbel Kindji, Meriam Maadi, Abdoulaye Mbaye, Claire Perroux, Ismaël Rousseau, Papa Séga Wadé, Gilles Xiberras, Olivier Zhang, Malek Zitouni
nodes.summary: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

nodes.title: Forecasting Brand Mentions in LLM Answers: Frozen Predictions Evaluated from Hours to Weeks
nodes.authors: Dmitrij Żatuchin
nodes.summary: Companies and agencies now monitor which brands large language models (LLMs) name when buyers ask for recommendations. Answers vary between runs, so a single check can mislead and repeated checks cost money. We extend an earlier 20-day replication to ask how well past brand mentions predict later ones over seven weeks. We froze probabilistic forecasts before each of four prospective collection waves of Gemini 3.1 Pro answers to the same 54 buyer questions: nine question families in English, Estonian and Finnish, each for two markets, with four of 12 tracked brands per question. The waves were collected between 1.5 hours and 52 days after the history used by the earliest forecast, and each scored 648 brand and answer labels from 162 answers. A smoothed per-question history achieved a Brier score of 0.0599 at 1.5 hours, against 0.1131 for a per-brand rate and 0.25 for a constant 0.5. A pooled rate clipped to 0.05--0.95, named as the challenger before its first test, scored 0.0259 after 8 hours, 0.0269 after 30 days and 0.0328 after 52 days. Of the brand and question cells named in all or none of the earlier answers, 94.5% to 97.5% kept that pattern in each later wave, and none switched from always to never or back. With a search instruction, 100 of 162 answers returned search activity, compared with 1 of 540 earlier Pro answers; mentions stayed predictable (Brier 0.0563), and Pro history predicted a smaller model's answers less well (0.0787). Human coding agreed with 298/300 sampled automatic labels; two coders agreed on 99/100 shared items (kappa = 0.98). The results cover one provider family, a fixed candidate set and lexical mentions. They support per-question history as the baseline that any forecasting or monitoring method for LLM brand mentions should beat.

nodes.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
nodes.authors: Zichen Zhu, Dingye Liu, Nan Jiang, Danyang Zhang, Hang Zheng, Shijie Zheng, Situo Zhang, Kunyao Lan, Yingzi Ma, Sheng Jiang, Lu Chen, Kai Yu
nodes.summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

nodes.title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
nodes.authors: Dmytro Babarytskyi
nodes.summary: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.

nodes.title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
nodes.authors: Chia-Ming Lee, Yu-Jou Hsiao, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Chung Hsu
nodes.summary: Hyperspectral images (HSI) preserve material evidence lost in RGB, yet 3D material identification from multi-view HSI faces two obstacles. Spectral Gaussian splatting reconstructs spectra accurately but leaves unmixing to per-pixel post-processing, while multi-view hyperspectral capture is costly and real datasets lack pixel-level material labels and sub-pixel proportions. We propose Spectral World Renderer (SWR), a material-aware explicit representation that unifies 3D spectral reconstruction and unmixing: it fits a Gaussian scaffold from RGB and decodes ray-Gaussian intersections into abundances over a shared endmember dictionary. Additionally, appearance guidance prevents spectrally similar materials from merging when intensity absorbs their brightness differences. Moreover, SWR requires no material-label supervision during training. To address the data gap, we further construct the SWR Benchmark (SWR-Bench): a coding-agent pipeline generates eight indoor and outdoor worlds from measured reflectance, aligning HSI with both annotations. SWR achieves the highest mIoU in all eight worlds and the highest mean PSNR on each real dataset. On an 11-class urban world, it trains at least 3.67x faster than unmixing baselines; rendering averages 34.9 joint spectral and label views/s over four worlds on a single RTX 4090.

nodes.title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
nodes.authors: Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thales Sales Almeida, Marcelo da Silva Reis, Rodrigo Nogueira, Marcos Meideiros Raimundo
nodes.summary: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
nodes.authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
nodes.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: CALM: Decentralized Control of Cooperative Aerial Manipulation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
nodes.authors: Jiaxi Huo, Petre Ricioppo, Fausto Francesco Lizzio
nodes.summary: Cooperative aerial manipulation is difficult under wind, payload motion, and noisy goal broadcasts because multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are coupled through a shared payload. We present CALM (Cooperative Aerial Learned Manipulation), a decentralized controller for aerial manipulators carrying a basket while tracking a moving ground robot. CALM combines a parameter-shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policy, trained using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), with goal estimation, per-UAV Extended State Observers (ESOs), basket-mass estimation, and anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward. The anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward uses estimated goal motion to rotate the formation before position error develops, reducing basket-yaw lag without adding net commanded force. A disturbance-conditioned critic supports centralized training while execution remains decentralized. Across held-out trajectories, CALM achieves lower mean position and orientation errors than all evaluated baselines, including the matched arm baseline (7.68 versus 10.95 cm and 3.3 versus 4.7$^\circ$), the cable-suspended realization, and two model-based controllers. Under unseen full-information-path degradation, CALM remains statistically comparable or superior to the arm baseline. Videos are available at https://petreric.github.io/CALM/.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
nodes.authors: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang, Stef Ren, Jianwen Xie, Jiajun Wu, Li Fei-Fei, Ruohan Zhang
nodes.summary: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks.
